edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De corona militis, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Proxime facta est liberalitas praestantissimorum imperatorum; expungebantur in castris milites laureati. Adhibetur quidam illic magis Dei miles, caeteris constantior fratribus, qui se duobus dominis servire posse praesumpserant, solus libero eapite, coronamento in manu otioso. Vulgata jam et ista disciplina Christianorum relucebat. Denique singuli designare, et eludere eminus, infrendere cominus. Murmur tribuno defertur, et persona jam ex ordine accesserat. Statim tribunus: Cur, inquit, tam diversus habitu? Negavit ille cum caeteris sibi licere; caussas expostulatus, Christianus sum, respondit. O militem in Deo gloriosum! Suffragia exinde, et res ampliata, et reus ad praefectos. Ibidem gravissimas penulas posuit, relevari auspicatus, speculatoriam morosissimam de pedibus absolvit, terrae sanctae insistere incipiens, gladium nec dominicae defensioni necessarium reddidit: laurea et de manu corruit. Et nunc russatus sanguinis sui spe, calceatus de Evangelii paratura, succinctus acutiore verbo Dei, totus de Apostolo armatus et de martyrii candida melius coronandus, donativum Christi in carcere exspectat. Exinde sententiae super illo, nescio an Christianorum, non enim aliae ethnicorum, ut de abrupto, et praecipiti, et mori cupido, qui de habitu interrogatus nomini negotium fecerit: solus scilicet fortis, inter tot fratres commilitones solus Christianus. Plane superest ut etiam martyria recusare meditentur, qui prophetias ejusdem Spiritus sancti respuerunt. Mussitant denique, tam bonam et longam sibi pacem periclitari. Nec dubito quosdam Scripturas emigrare, sarcinas expedire, fugae accingi de civitate in civitatem; nullam enim aliam Evangelii memoriam curant. Novi et pastores corum, in pace leones, in praelio cervos. Sed de quaestionibus confessionum alibi docebimus. At nunc quatenus et illud opponunt: Ubi autem prohibemur coronari? Hanc magis localem substantiam caussae praesentis aggrediar, ut et qui ex sollicitudine ignorantiae quaerunt, instruantur; et qui in defensionem delicti contendunt, revincantur; ipsi vel maxime Christiani laureati, quibus id solum quaestio est; quasi aut nullum aut incertum saltem haberi possit delictum quod patiatur quaestionem. Nec nullum autem nec incertum, hinc interim ostendam.
thought_title: The Christian and the Laurel Wreath
pass_a_gloss: Recently there was a generosity of the most excellent emperors; the soldiers who were crowned were being discharged from the camp. A certain soldier of God was present there, more constant than the other brothers, who had presumed that he could serve two lords, alone with his head free, with a laurel wreath idle in his hand. Now this discipline of the Christians was already well-known. Finally, the individual soldiers were pointing him out and mocking him from a distance and sneering at him up close. A murmur was reported to the tribune, and the person had already been summoned in order. Immediately the tribune said: Why are you so different in appearance? He denied that it was permitted for him to do as the others did; when asked for a reason, he responded: I am a Christian. O glorious soldier in God! From then on, there were votes and the matter was enlarged, and the accused was brought before the prefects. There, he put aside the very heavy packs, having dared to be relieved, he released the most troublesome sentinel duty from his feet, beginning to stand on holy ground, he did not consider the sword necessary for the Lord's defense: the laurel wreath also fell from his hand. And now, having been spattered with the hope of his own blood, shod with the preparation of the Gospel, girded with the sharper word of God, fully armed with the Apostle and better crowned with the white of martyrdom, he awaits the gift of Christ in prison. From then on, the opinions about him, I do not know whether of the Christians, for certainly not of the others of the gentiles, as if from a precipice, and steep, and desiring to die, who having been asked about his appearance made it a matter of his name: alone certainly strong, among so many brother soldiers alone a Christian. Clearly, it remains that they also intend to refuse martyrdom, who have rejected the prophecies of the same Holy Spirit. They are murmuring, finally, that such a good and long peace is being put in danger for them. And I do not doubt that some are preparing to migrate, to pack their bags, to gird themselves for flight from city to city; for they do not care about any other memory of the Gospel. And I know their shepherds, lions in peace, deer in battle. But we will teach about the questions of confessions elsewhere. Now, however, as far as they oppose this: Where are we forbidden to be crowned? I will attack this more local substance of the present cause, so that both those who ask out of anxious ignorance may be instructed, and those who strive in defense of the offense may be overcome; especially the Christian soldiers who are crowned, for whom this is the only question; as if there could be no offense or at least an uncertain one that could suffer a question. And I will show that it is neither none nor uncertain, at least for now.

pass_b_english: The most excellent emperors have just shown their generosity: laureled veterans were being discharged from camp. Among them stood a soldier of God, steadier in his faith than the rest of the brothers—men who had presumed they could serve two masters. He alone stood bareheaded, the laurel wreath lying idle in his hand. By now the Christians' discipline was an open secret. The other soldiers began singling him out, jeering from a distance and sneering to his face. A murmur reached the tribune, and the man was summoned at once. The tribune demanded, "Why do you look so different?" He replied that he was not permitted to do as the others did. Pressed for a reason, he answered: "I am a Christian." What a glorious soldier of God! From that moment the votes were cast, the charge escalated, and the accused was hauled before the prefects. There he threw down the crushing packs, daring to be relieved of them; he shook the most wretched sentinel duty from his feet, stepping onto holy ground. He declared the sword unnecessary for the Lord's defense, and the laurel fell from his hand as well. Now, spattered with the hope of his own blood, shod with the Gospel's readiness, girded with the sharper Word of God, fully armed with the Apostle, and better crowned with the white of martyrdom, he awaits Christ's gift in prison.

Opinions flew fast after that—whether from Christians I cannot say, but certainly not from the pagans. They acted as if pushed from a cliff, steep and headlong, desperate to die, all because a man questioned about his uniform made it a matter of his Name. Alone he was brave; among so many brother-soldiers, he alone was a Christian. Clearly those who have spat on the prophecies of the same Holy Spirit now intend to refuse martyrdom too. They are muttering that their good, long peace is being endangered. I have no doubt some are already preparing to emigrate, packing bags, girding themselves for flight from city to city, since they care nothing for any other memory of the Gospel. I know their shepherds: lions in peace, deer in battle. We will settle the questions of confessions elsewhere. But right now I must meet their objection: "Where are we forbidden to be crowned?" I will tackle the concrete substance of this case so that both those who ask from anxious ignorance may be instructed and those who fight to defend the offense may be confounded—especially the crowned Christian soldiers, for whom this is the only question, as if the offense were either nonexistent or at least uncertain. It is neither; I will prove that much for now.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent, high-quality rendering that preserves all nuances, including the distinction between 'Christianorum' and 'ethnicorum' (pagans), the specific imagery of the soldier's equipment, and the rhetorical structure of the concluding argument. All theological and legal nuances (e.g., 'delictum' as offense/charge, 'confessionum' as confessions) are maintained.
